title: Intermolecular Forces, Polarity and Gases
seo_title: Year 11 Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces and Gases Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Chemistry Unit 2: Intermolecular forces and gases
standard_text: Dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding; polarity from bond polarity and shape; boiling points and solubility; the kinetic molecular theory, the gas laws and the ideal gas equation pV = nRT. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 2: Molecular interactions and reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Chemistry worksheets on intermolecular forces: dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding, polarity, boiling points, solubility, Boyle's and Charles' laws and pV = nRT. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point.
key_sub: pV = nRT with T in kelvin; R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
body_html:
How to think about it

Molecules attract each other by dispersion forces (all molecules, stronger for more electrons), dipole–dipole forces (polar molecules) and hydrogen bonds (H on N, O or F). These forces, not the covalent bonds, are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.

A molecule is polar if its bonds are polar and its shape does not cancel them (H₂O is polar, CO₂ is not). Gases follow pV = nRT: pressure rises if volume falls (Boyle) and volume rises with kelvin temperature (Charles).

Example

A gas at 100 kPa is squeezed from 6.0 L to 2.0 L (same T). New pressure?

p₁V₁ = p₂V₂

100 × 6.0 ÷ 2.0

Answer: 300 kPa

Example

Moles of gas in 2.48 L at 100 kPa and 298 K?

n = pV ÷ RT

100 × 2.48 ÷ (8.31 × 298)

Answer: 0.100 mol

Common mistakes

  • Saying covalent bonds break when water boils: hydrogen bonds between molecules are overcome.
  • Using °C in the gas laws.
  • Calling every molecule with polar bonds a polar molecule.

faq.a: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open lattice in ice, so ice is less dense than liquid water.

faq.q: When is a gas most like an ideal gas?
faq.a: At low pressure and high temperature, where the particles are far apart and move fast, so their volume and attractions hardly matter.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Nonpolar particles only have intermolecular forces.

items.q: Why can metals be hammered into shape?
c: layers of positive ions can slide over each other
the electrons are fixed in place
items.e: The delocalised electrons hold the ions together as layers slide.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of water (H<sub>2</sub>O)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: H bonded to N, O or F gives hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Which molecule can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself?
items.e: H must be bonded to N, O or F.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Nonpolar particles only have intermolecular forces.

items.q: What does the kinetic molecular theory say about gas particles?
c: they all move at the same speed
they move randomly and rapidly, and their mean kinetic energy depends on temperature
items.e: Collisions with the walls cause pressure.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of magnesium oxide (MgO)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Ions attract each other strongly.

items.q: Which intermolecular force is present between all molecules?
items.e: Dispersion forces come from temporary dipoles.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Nonpolar particles only have intermolecular forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of potassium chloride (KCl)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Ions attract each other strongly.

items.q: Why does water have a higher boiling point than H₂S?
items.e: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the other intermolecular forces in H₂S.

items.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
c: ice contains air bubbles in every case
hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice
items.e: So ice floats and lakes freeze from the top.

items.q: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force?
items.e: Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of sodium chloride (NaCl)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Ions attract each other strongly.

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: many strong covalent bonds must be broken
items.e: Diamond is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of chloromethane (CH<sub>3</sub>Cl)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Polar molecules without H bonded to N, O or F have dipole-dipole forces.

items.q: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
items.e: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.

items.q: Why is water a polar molecule?
c: its O–H bonds are polar and its bent shape means the dipoles do not cancel
oxygen and hydrogen share electrons equally
items.e: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen.

items.q: Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
items.e: Ions are fixed in the solid but free to move when molten.

items.q: Which temperature scale must be used in gas law calculations?
c: any scale, as long as it is the same throughout
the scale printed on the thermometer

items.q: Electronegativity: nitrogen (N) = 3.04 and boron (B) = 2.04. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.00. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Electronegativity: bromine (Br) = 2.96 and phosphorus (P) = 2.19. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.77. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Why is water's boiling point (100 °C) much higher than that of H₂S (−60 °C)?
c: water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
items.e: H₂S has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

items.q: Why is CO₂ a non-polar molecule even though its C=O bonds are polar?
c: carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
it is linear, so the bond dipoles cancel
items.e: Molecular shape decides overall polarity.

items.q: What is the bond angle in H<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of CO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: linear.

items.q: What happens to the pressure of a gas if its volume is halved at constant temperature?
items.e: Boyle's law: pV is constant.

items.q: What is the bond angle in XeF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: In a bond between phosphorus (P) and chlorine (Cl) (electronegativities 2.19 and 3.16), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: What is the shape of SF<sub>6</sub>?
items.e: 6 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: octahedral.

items.q: What is the bond angle in SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: In a bond between chlorine (Cl) and carbon (C) (electronegativities 3.16 and 2.55), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: Why does the boiling point of the alkanes increase as the chain gets longer?
c: covalent bonds in the chain break
larger molecules have more electrons, so dispersion forces are stronger
items.e: Methane is a gas; octane is a liquid.

items.q: Why does a gas behave less ideally at high pressure?
c: the particles are close together, so their own volume and attractions matter
items.e: Ideal gases have no volume and no attractions.

items.q: What is the shape of BF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: trigonal planar.

items.q: Why does hexane not dissolve in water?
c: hexane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
items.e: Water molecules attract each other more strongly.

items.q: What is the bond angle in CO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: Electronegativity: chlorine (Cl) = 3.16 and silicon (Si) = 1.90. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.26. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: What is the shape of PCl<sub>5</sub>?
items.e: 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: trigonal bipyramidal.

items.q: Electronegativity: nitrogen (N) = 3.04 and chlorine (Cl) = 3.16. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.12. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, hydrogen fluoride (HF) or phosphine (PH<sub>3</sub>)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Hydrogen fluoride has hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in phosphine.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, argon (Ar) or butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; butane is larger (58 g/mol vs 40 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: A gas occupies 1.00 L at 15 °C. It is heated to 127 °C at constant pressure. Calculate its new volume.
items.e: V/T is constant with T in kelvin: V₂ = 1.00 × 400/288 = 1.39 L.

items.q: A gas occupies 2.50 L at 27 °C. It is heated to 227 °C at constant pressure. Calculate its new volume.
items.e: V/T is constant with T in kelvin: V₂ = 2.50 × 500/300 = 4.17 L.

items.e: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, p₂ = 800 kPa.

items.e: n = pV/(RT) = 0.500 mol; Mr = m/n = 28.0 (N2).
